safety.title: Safety comes first
safety.body: Make the next step about immediate safety, not resolving the whole situation. If anyone may be in danger or you suspect an overdose, call emergency services now.

overloaded.title: Make today's plan smaller
overloaded.body: You're carrying heavy pressure with very little capacity. Focus on one safe next step, one boundary, and one person who can support you.

connection.title: Do not carry today alone
connection.body: Choose one safe person and make a specific ask: ten minutes to listen, help with a task, or company while you make a call.

boundary.title: Choose the boundary you can hold
boundary.body: Use a short sentence, name what you will do, and avoid adding a consequence you cannot follow through on.

plan.title: Only plan the next decision
plan.body: Write down what is known, what must be decided today, and what can wait. Today's family pathway above can guide the next step.

rest.title: Reduce one demand
rest.body: Rest is part of staying steady. Delay one nonessential task and protect a small block of time that belongs to you.

steady.title: Protect the steadiness you have
steady.body: Use some of today's capacity on your own life — a meal, a walk, work, sleep, or contact with someone who knows you.

checkIn.milestone7: 🌱 Seven days of showing up for yourself. That consistency is how families heal.
checkIn.milestone30: 🌿 Thirty days. A month of steadiness — you are building something real.
checkIn.milestone90: 🌳 Ninety days. This is who you are now. We're honored to walk with you.
checkIn.graceUsed: Life happened one day this week — we held your streak for you. 💙

pathway.title: What helps in this phase

pathway.privacy: This private selection guides your content. It is not a score or diagnosis.

active_use.label: Active use
active_use.description: When use is active, the goal is less chaos and more safety — not winning an argument.
do: Confirm who you can call and where you can go if the home becomes unsafe.
Keep money, medications, keys, and important documents where only you can reach them.
Choose one clear boundary you can actually hold today.
avoid: Do not argue about substance use while they are intoxicated.
Do not give cash or erase a consequence just to make the moment quieter.
Do not investigate in a way that puts you or a child at risk.
expect: Denial, blame, or fast mood changes can happen; you do not have to resolve them tonight.
You may feel hyper-alert or guilty when you step back. That does not make the boundary wrong.
Promises may be sincere and still not be followed by action.

considering_treatment.label: Considering treatment
considering_treatment.description: Interest in help often comes with ambivalence. Prepare a small next step before the window opens.
do: Write down two realistic help options and the first call required for each.
Choose a calm, sober time and lead with one observable fact and one offer of help.
Decide what practical help you can offer — a ride or a call — without taking over.
avoid: Do not make threats or ultimatums you are not prepared to carry out.
Do not overwhelm them with a long list of programs in one conversation.
Do not turn the talk into a debate about labels or whether they are 'bad enough.'
expect: A person can want change and fear it at the same time.
The conversation may need to happen more than once.
Motivation can shift quickly, so a simple prepared option helps.

in_treatment.label: In treatment
in_treatment.description: Treatment gives the family room to steady itself too. Your work is support, boundaries, and your own recovery.
do: Ask the program what family education or support is available and what consent allows them to share.
Restart one routine that supports your sleep, meals, work, or connection.
Write down the boundaries that will still matter after treatment.
avoid: Do not try to manage the treatment plan from outside the program.
Do not demand private clinical details as proof that treatment is working.
Do not treat discharge as the finish line for recovery.
expect: Relief, anger, hope, and fear can all show up together.
Contact may be limited while the person focuses on care.
Early changes can be real and still uneven.

returning_home.label: Preparing to return home
returning_home.description: A planned transition is safer than an improvised one. Make expectations and responses clear before the first hard day.
do: Agree on basic home expectations, supports, and what happens if a boundary is crossed.
Update emergency contacts, safe places, medication storage, and overdose-response supplies.
Plan the first week: transportation, appointments, household roles, and quiet recovery time.
avoid: Do not wait for a crisis to decide how the household will respond.
Do not assign yourself the job of monitoring them every hour.
Do not remove outside support just because they are coming home.
expect: Transitions can bring excitement and tension at the same time.
Everyone may need time to adjust to new roles and routines.
Trust usually rebuilds more slowly than hope.

early_recovery_30.label: First 30 days
early_recovery_30.description: The first month is about structure, support, and safety. Stability matters more than dramatic promises.
do: Protect recovery routines and choose one small routine that steadies you too.
Decide how you will respond to one warning sign before it appears.
Notice and name one recovery action without demanding reassurance.
avoid: Do not treat every hard mood as proof of a return to use.
Do not loosen important boundaries because the first days are going well.
Do not make their recovery your full-time job.
expect: Sleep, energy, and mood can be uneven while routines form.
Boredom and household friction can rise when the initial relief fades.
Your nervous system may stay on alert even when things are calmer.

early_recovery_90.label: Days 31–90
early_recovery_90.description: As daily life returns, protect the routines that work and rebuild trust in small, observable steps.
do: Hold one calm weekly check-in about routines, needs, and household responsibilities.
Rebuild one shared activity that does not revolve around recovery talk.
Recognize consistent behavior, not just intentions or promises.
avoid: Do not rush to restore money, access, or responsibilities before trust is ready.
Do not stop your own support because the immediate crisis has eased.
Do not confuse several good weeks with finished recovery work.
expect: Confidence may grow faster than stability.
Old relationship tension may surface now that the crisis is quieter.
New routines can still be fragile around stress, conflict, or isolation.

ongoing_recovery.label: Ongoing recovery
ongoing_recovery.description: Longer-term recovery still benefits from honest connection, durable boundaries, and a life that belongs to each person.
do: Keep one boundary and one support practice active even during a calm stretch.
Review the household safety plan and contact list before you need them.
Make room for a relationship moment that is not about addiction or recovery.
avoid: Do not abandon the plan simply because things have been well.
Do not pressure recovery to follow your preferred timeline.
Do not use sobriety to dismiss unresolved feelings or relationship repair.
expect: Milestones can bring grief or anxiety alongside pride.
Relationships can have setbacks without a return to substance use.
The kind of support each person needs may change over time.

return_to_use.label: Return to use
return_to_use.description: A return to use is serious, especially after abstinence. Move from shock to safety, facts, and the next available support.
do: Assess immediate danger and use your safety plan; call emergency services for a suspected overdose or immediate threat.
State what you observed in simple facts and follow the boundary you already set.
Contact your own support person and gather the next appropriate care option.
avoid: Do not shame, lecture, or try to force insight in the middle of intoxication.
Do not physically block someone from leaving or put yourself in harm's way.
Do not hide a suspected overdose or delay emergency help.
expect: Panic, grief, anger, or numbness are common family reactions.
Risk can change quickly, and tolerance may be lower after abstinence.
This setback does not erase prior recovery, but the next safe action matters now.

unsure.label: Not sure yet
unsure.description: Uncertainty is exhausting. Start with safety and observable facts instead of trying to solve the whole story today.
do: Write down only what you directly saw or heard, with a date and time.
Check your own body and the household for immediate safety concerns.
Choose one trusted person you can speak with without needing to prove anything.
avoid: Do not make an accusation when you only have a feeling or one ambiguous sign.
Do not search, follow, or confront in a way that could put you at risk.
Do not dismiss your concern just because you do not have certainty.
expect: Not knowing can keep your nervous system on high alert.
One sign by itself usually does not prove substance use.
Clarity may come from a pattern of facts rather than one conversation.

dailyQuote.0: You didn't cause it, you can't control it, you can't cure it.
dailyQuote.1: Caring for yourself is the most powerful thing you can do for your family.
dailyQuote.2: Progress, not perfection, is the goal.
dailyQuote.3: You cannot save someone who doesn't want to be saved — but you can stay whole.
dailyQuote.4: Your limits are not punishments. They are your values made visible.
dailyQuote.5: The only way out is through — together.
dailyQuote.6: Love the person. Decline the chaos.
dailyQuote.7: Recovery happens in community, not isolation.
dailyQuote.8: Setting a limit is an act of love.
dailyQuote.9: Holding your ground is how you show up.
dailyQuote.10: You are not the disease. Neither is your family.
dailyQuote.11: Every day you stay steady is a day you model recovery for someone who is watching.
dailyQuote.12: Let go of what you cannot control. Hold on to what matters.
dailyQuote.13: Boundaries create the space where healing can happen.
